passages.t: The Lord beside the altar, and no place to hide
passages.happening:
‘I saw the Lord standing beside the altar’ (verse 1). He commands the tops of the pillars to be struck so that the thresholds shake and the building falls on the people. None who flee will get away.

‘Though they dig down to Sheol, from there My hand will take them; and though they climb up to heaven, from there I will pull them down’ (verse 2). If they hide on the top of Carmel or at the bottom of the sea, or are driven into captivity by their enemies, God will find them there (verses 3-4).

The Lord GOD of Hosts touches the earth and it melts. He builds his upper rooms in the heavens and pours out the waters of the sea on the earth. ‘The LORD is His name’ (verses 5-6).
passages.hearers:
The altar is not named, but the book suggests the royal sanctuary at Bethel, where Amos faced Amaziah and whose altars he had said would be cut down. In the fifth vision, Amos sees the Lord himself at the very place where Israel thought it was safe.

Verses 2 to 4 are a poem of pursuit with five clauses, though they dig, though they climb, though they hide, each answered by God's reach. It is a dark mirror of the psalm in which the same truth comforts: there is nowhere God is not. For a people who have made his altar a place of injustice, that truth is a terror.

Verses 5 and 6 are the third of Amos's hymns to the Creator, each ending with the LORD's name. The northern kingdom fell to Assyria in 722 BC, and its people were deported and scattered.
passages.later: A psalm says the same thing as comfort: ‘If I ascend to the heavens, You are there; if I make my bed in Sheol, You are there’ (Psalm 139:8). Amos had said the horns of Bethel's altar would be cut off (Amos 3:14).
passages.asks: There is nowhere to hide from God. Ask whether that truth feels like a threat or a comfort to you, and why. And ask what you have been trying to keep out of his sight.

passages.happening:
‘Are you not like the Cushites to Me, O children of Israel?’ declares the LORD (verse 7). He brought Israel up from Egypt, and also the Philistines from Caphtor and the Arameans from Kir.

The eyes of the Lord GOD are on the sinful kingdom, and he will destroy it from the face of the earth. ‘Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob,’ declares the LORD (verse 8). He will shake Israel among the nations as grain is shaken in a sieve, but not a pebble will fall to the ground (verse 9). All the sinners among his people who say disaster will never come near them will die by the sword (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Verse 7 names peoples at the edges of Israel's world. The Cushites lived south of Egypt, in the region of modern Sudan, and stood for the far ends of the earth. Caphtor is usually identified with Crete and the Aegean, where the Philistines were believed to have come from. Kir, whose location is uncertain, was remembered as the homeland of the Arameans. Amos's point is startling. Israel's exodus was a real act of God, but God had also directed the movements of Israel's neighbors. The exodus did not make Israel immune.

The sieve was used after threshing to separate grain from stones. The picture is debated: either the pebbles are the wicked, caught and kept for judgment, or the kernels are the faithful, none of which will be lost.

Verse 8 holds two things together. The sinful kingdom will be destroyed, but the house of Jacob will not be utterly destroyed. Those who will die are those who say that disaster will never touch them.
passages.later: God's care reaches every people: ‘The LORD is good to all; His compassion rests on all He has made’ (Psalm 145:9). Isaiah too foresaw a remnant that would return (Isaiah 10:20-22).
passages.hard:
What does it mean that Israel is like the Cushites to God?

The verse is not saying that Israel's history with God meant nothing. The rest of the book takes the exodus and the covenant seriously. It is saying that Israel had turned its election into a claim of immunity, as if being brought out of Egypt meant disaster could not touch it (verse 10). God answers that he is the God of every nation's history, not only Israel's. Being chosen was a calling, not a shield.

Readers have heard in this verse both a warning to anyone who treats God's grace as a guarantee, and a reminder that the distant peoples Israel looked down on were also under God's care. It gives no people, then or now, a reason to think of itself as above others before God.
passages.asks: Israel thought being chosen meant disaster could never reach it. Ask what you have been counting on as a guarantee that God owes you. And ask who you have thought of as far from God, whom he has been caring for all along.

passages.t: The fallen tent of David rebuilt
passages.happening:
‘In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David. I will repair its gaps, restore its ruins, and rebuild it as in the days of old’ (verse 11), so that they may possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear God's name (verse 12).

The days are coming when the plowman will catch up with the reaper, and the one treading grapes with the one sowing seed. The mountains will drip with sweet wine (verse 13). ‘I will restore My people Israel from captivity; they will rebuild and inhabit the ruined cities. They will plant vineyards and drink their wine; they will make gardens and eat their fruit’ (verse 14). God will plant them in their land, never again to be uprooted (verse 15).
passages.hearers:
The fallen tent of David has been read in two main ways. Many scholars think it assumes the fall of Jerusalem and the end of David's dynasty in 587 or 586 BC, and so regard verses 11 to 15 as an addition from the time of the exile, completing the book for later readers. Others argue that it fits Amos's own day: David's kingdom had been split since about 930 BC, and his house ruled only small Judah, so a prophet in the eighth century could call it fallen and promise its reunion. Both agree that the promise speaks of a renewed kingdom of David reaching beyond Judah.

The closing pictures come from the farmer's year. The harvest is so large that the plowing for the next season begins before the reaping is done. The judgments of the book are reversed: the curse that they would build stone houses and not live in them, and plant vineyards and not drink their wine, is undone.

These are promises to Israel after the exile, in the words of an eighth-century prophet. They make no claim about any modern state or border.
passages.later: At the council in Jerusalem, James quoted verses 11 and 12 in their Greek form: ‘After this I will return and rebuild the fallen tent of David’ (Acts 15:16), ‘so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name’ (Acts 15:17). Amos had warned, ‘you will never drink the wine from the lush vineyards you have planted’ (Amos 5:11).
passages.hard:
Why does Amos speak of Israel possessing Edom, while Acts 15 speaks of all people seeking the Lord?

The Hebrew of Amos says the restored house of David will possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear God's name. The Greek translation, which James follows in Acts 15:17, reads so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord. The two reflect very similar Hebrew words: Edom and adam, humankind, and possess, yarash, and seek, darash. Some scholars think the Greek reflects a different Hebrew text; others think the translators interpreted the passage.

Many interpreters point out that even the Hebrew speaks of nations that bear God's name, that is, who belong to him, so both readings picture the nations included in David's kingdom rather than simply conquered. Many conclude that James's argument does not rest on the Greek alone, though others think the Greek wording carries more of the weight.
passages.asks: The book that began with a lion's roar ends with vineyards replanted. Ask what ruins in your own life you have given up on that God might rebuild. And James read this promise as room for all nations in David's house. Ask who you have assumed has no place there.
